newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Absa fund manager cautious on 1997 SAfrica returns.
newsitem.headline: Absa fund manager cautious on 1997 SAfrica returns.

text.p: South African markets will generate mundane returns in the first half of 1997 but should improve in the second half if the rand stabilises as expected, Absa Asset Management said on Friday.
General manager Malcolm Chapman said he was expecting real, after-inflation returns on a portfolio of South African assets of five percent this year against some 10 percent in 1996.
With the economy set to slow in 1997, corporate earnings growth of stocks in Absa's portfolio were likely to decline to 15-18 percent in 1997 from 23-25 percent in 1996, he told Reuters.
But the second half of the year should see returns improve as investors look to a brighter 1998.
"We're looking at the first half being a little slower than last year but we are looking at a good second half," he said.
"Cash may be king but gilts and equities should produce good returns in the second half of the year."
Absa's asset allocation for a balanced portfolio is currently running at 60 percent equities, 30 percent fixed income and 10 percent cash.

A key factor in 1997 will be foreigners' perception of South Africa, Chapman said. At present most international fund managers of MSCI and IFC Index global funds remain significnatly underweight in South African equities.

"Some did come in early and lost money on the exchange rate. They are going to look at it very, very carefully and I think the dollar/rand exchange rate is going to play a very important role in their decision-making process," he said.
"But in due course our market is going to look cheap and then they will definitely come in."
Like many other analysts, Chapman sees the rand weakening further in 1997 but at a much slower pace than in 1996 when it slumped 29 percent against the dollar.
He said he expected strong support for the rand at 4.95 to the dollar. The currency was trading on Friday at around 4.66.

Other limiting factors for South African stocks in 1997 were likely to be continued concerns about the future of exchange controls and further asset swaps between local and international institutions which would reduce the market "greenhouse effect".
Historically, the Johannesburg Stock Exchange has been buoyed by a pool of pension fund and life insurance money that had nowhere else to go.

But the ability of local institutions to take a portion of funds offshore, following recent moves to ease exchange controls, means some money that would normally go to the JSE will now be going elsewhere, Chapman said.
